transcript: On the moonless night of October 29th, 1914, two Ottoman cruisers sneak into the harbor of Odessa. Once in position, the crew loads a torpedo and launches it at an unexpecting gunboat. For half an hour, they wreak havoc on the port. While not all in Constantinople are pleased, the Black Sea raid makes Turkish entry into the war inevitable. Two weeks later, the Sultan of the Empire declares a jihad or holy war against the Anton powers of the First World War. Ottoman participation in the great war had been a long time coming. 2 months before shelling Russian ports, the empire formally allied with Germany, shielded German ships from the Antant, and even closed the Turkish straits to British shipping. The Middle Eastern theater would see vicious fighting in treacherous conditions with its legacy shaping the modern Middle East. After entering the war, Ottoman attention immediately shifted to their mountainous border with the Russian Empire. Here they hoped to recover lost territory while also relieving pressure off their allies in Poland. Enver Pasha, the Ottoman Minister of War, engaged the Russian army near Sarakamish in eastern Anatolia at a high altitude of 6,000 ft or 1,800 m. The result was devastating. The Russian counterattack encircled the Ottoman Third Army, leaving only a fraction of Ottoman forces to make it back to their headquarters at Arzarum. The battle of Sarah Kamish was indicative of the entire Middle Eastern theater. The armies were comparatively small, but environmental and logistical problems wre havoc on the armies. In the Caucus' mountains, Frostbite and Typhus claimed as many lives as combat. The strain of supporting fighting in remote areas drained the local population of resources, leading to widespread famine and disease. Additionally, Enver Pasha in particular blamed his chaotic defeat on the disloyalty of the area's ethnic minority, in this case, the Armenians. The war in the Caucasus represented an existential fight for the Ottomans. It was here that the empire directed most of its attention and resources. Meanwhile, the Mesopotamian front initially began as a small frontier style operation when British Indian troops seized control of Bassra, an important trade hub. Boooied by this success, Britain pushed further into Mesopotamia. In Egypt, it was the Ottoman army which took the initiative. Led by Jeml Pasha and the German general Friedrich Cres vancresenstein, an army crossed the Sinai Peninsula in January 1915 to disrupt the Suez Canal and sever Britain's trade with its colonial subjects. Although the raid was beaten back by Indian defenders, the Ottomans continued to threaten the canal. Aside from the main fronts, the war spilled over into neutral nations. Iran notably never fought in the war, but the war was certainly fought in it. Russian and British forces brawled with Ottoman and German ones as both sought to undermine the enemy's local influence. German agents, notably Wilhelm Vasmos, organized and led revolts against Britain. The fighting in Iran devastated the country and left 2 million civilians dead. The Ottoman Empire got itself into a three-front war. However, none of these fronts seemed to directly threaten the empire's heartland, which was thousands of miles away from Constantinople. That changed on April 25th, 1915 as the Antant thrust a dagger right into the Turkish Straits. Britain's first lord of the admiral team, Winston Churchill, devised an audacious plan to force a passage through the Dinell Strait, coerced the Ottomans to sue for peace and reopen a supply route to Russia. An initial naval attack in March failed miserably, and by April, the plan morphed into an amphibious assault to clear the Ottoman defenses in the area. The Turks were prepared under supervision of the German general Ado Leman vonanders. An ingenious defense in depth system turned the peninsula into an impregnable fortress. transcript: Waves of US Marines packed the landing zones on Betio Island, pushing forward step by step. They advance into a hail of bullets, trapped in the deadly crossfire from entrenched Japanese positions. Though they vastly outnumber the Japanese Special Landing Forces defending the island, US forces face 76 hours of hellish combat. Obstacles and pillboxes cluttered the island where 1,500 Americans lie dead on the first day. The bloody morning of Tarawa marks the first contested landing of the island-hopping campaign against the Japanese Empire. Long before American forces waded ashore on Pacific atolls, US military planners had anticipated a potential conflict in the region. Starting in 1906, the US Naval War College and the Joint Planning Committee developed a series of plans for hostilities against the rising Japanese Empire, code-named War Plan Orange. The plan envisioned a decisive naval battle near the Philippines if the Japanese Navy struck this US-held territory. American battleships and cruisers would deploy from their naval bases in the Pacific to rescue their outnumbered allies, and together they would pound the Japanese fleet into submission. The Joint Planning Committee revised War Plan Orange nine times before ultimately scrapping it in the 1930s. Both the Army and the Navy's thinking evolved in response to new strategic realities. For one, Orange assumed US naval superiority was a given, yet the Imperial Japanese Navy gained valuable experience during the First World War and expanded significantly after renouncing the Washington Naval Treaty. The Japanese seizure of German [music] colonies in the South Pacific created a potential barrier to US shipping lanes to the Philippines. Japanese warships could concentrate their forces and fight US fleets before they could be reinforced from their far-flung territories. Meanwhile, advances in weapon systems challenged the supremacy of heavily armed battleship formations. Submarines could stalk and US squadrons over long distances. Even heavily [music] armored warships could fall prey to repeated aerial attacks without air support. Officers in the US Marine Corps proposed an incremental campaign across the Pacific rather than a single climactic battle. In 1923 operations plan, Lieutenant Colonel Earl Hancock Ellis advocated [music] for rapid amphibious landings supported by naval bombardment and aircraft providing cover [music] to seize enemy shores. He noted that specific island chains were to [music] be secured and estimated the manpower and equipment requirements to accomplish the operations. Once captured, these islands would serve as forward bases from which the Navy could launch offensive operations deeper into [music] Japanese held territory. December 7th, 1941 shattered any remaining illusions about a single decisive battle deciding the war. The Philippines fell soon after and US Army General Douglas MacArthur was forced to turn tail. Japanese task forces soon captured other American territories like Guam and Wake Island along with hundreds of POWs. The Japanese Empire expanded rapidly into the South and West, even threatening an invasion of Australia. However, by late 1942, US naval and air forces dealt heavy blows to the Imperial Japanese Navy during the battles of Midway and the Coral Sea. Forced to recoup its losses, Japanese expansion ground to a halt. Although the United States now had an opportunity to strike back and the American public was eager to take the war to Japan, President Franklin D. Roosevelt's promise to Churchill to prioritize the European theater delayed the Pacific offensive. A complex set of problems stood in the way of the US Navy and Army. The first was distance. The Pacific theater was enormous, many times larger than the European theater. The US and Japan conducted a war in an area that spanned tens of millions of square kilometers.
